title: 17 Signs You're Losing Control Of Your Class
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Michael Linsin argues that classroom control is lost gradually through small, ignorable warning signs long before a class becomes visibly unmanageable, and that teachers who wait until the obvious crisis point face a far harder fix than those who intervene early. His central claim is diagnostic rather than corrective: he offers 17 specific, observable signs — from transitions taking longer than 30 seconds to needing to bribe students into compliance to students laughing while the teacher is serious — designed to help teachers recognize decline while it is still small and reversible. Linsin's prescribed response is deliberately drastic relative to the size of the warning sign: the moment any sign appears, stop everything, return to the previous transition, and reteach the expectation 'in exacting detail,' rather than pushing forward and hoping the issue resolves itself. He frames this relentless, moment-to-moment correction — checking for what he calls a 'wet finger in the air' sensitivity to anything amiss — as the actual mechanism behind calm, well-managed classrooms, rather than any single policy or consequence system. The piece's underlying argument is that classroom management is won or lost in accumulated small moments, not in dramatic interventions after things have already broken down.
points: Linsin's framing that 'trying to gain control of an already out-of-control class is exceptionally difficult' while catching early signs is comparatively easy reframes classroom management as a detection problem as much as a correction problem.

The specificity of signs like 'transitions take longer than 30 seconds' and 'you have to bribe your students into compliance' gives teachers concrete, checkable benchmarks rather than a vague sense that 'things feel off,' making early self-diagnosis actionable.

His prescribed response — stopping everything and reteaching the expectation 'in exacting detail' at the first sign of drift, rather than waiting to see if it resolves — treats consistency of correction, not severity of consequence, as the actual lever for maintaining control.
quotes: Most teachers respond to losing control too late. They wait until they can't even get their class quiet and seated before making changes.
It's far easier to recognize the signs that you're headed toward a cliff than it is to wait until you've reached terminal velocity.
So what follows are 17 signs you're definitely, 100 percent losing control of your class.

The moment you notice your class going off the rails, you must stop everything, return to the previous transition, and reteach what you expect in exacting detail—which may also include your classroom management plan.
Great teachers always have their wet finger in the air. If they sense anything amiss, however small or subtle, they reverse course immediately and fix it.
It's the relentless pursuit of success from one moment to the next that not only negates the possibility of losing control, but assures a calm, well-behaved classroom every day.
